findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: Responsive repairs budget cut to £26m despite year-to-date demand rising to 3.68 repairs per property
findings.detail: Repairs budget reduced 13% from £30m to £26m for 2026-27 after one-off £5.6m allocation. However actual year-to-date 2025-26 shows 3.68 average repairs per property, up from 2.9 prior year. Explained as 'temporarily inflated by catch-up repairs', but this represents demand pressure against a cost reduction.
findings.matters: Budget reduction against rising actual demand creates overspend risk; any variance against this tight forecast would require operational tightening or further borrowing in an already covenant-constrained position.
findings.figures: Budget cut £4m (to £26m); actual 2025-26 repairs per property 3.68 vs 2.9 prior year average
findings.quote: The 2025-26 responsive repairs budget of £30m had a one-off allocation of £5.6m to support the initiation of the new works programmes. This has been implemented and the tracking at activity levels has supported the decision to reduce the responsive repairs budget for 2026-27 of £26m... for 2025/26 the service is experiencing an increased year-to-date average of 3.68.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: Regina Road Phase 1 budget increased to £171m with further cost updates due early 2026 from main contractor procurement
findings.detail: Budget increased from previously agreed £166m to £171m reflecting 'latest assessment of current costs following further design development'. An updated cost plan is due early 2026 incorporating main contractor procurement outcomes. The budget 'remains under review and will be amended as detailed design evolves'.
findings.matters: Major capital scheme already showing £5m cost increase; significant uncertainty remains before final pricing, creating material risk of further escalation.
findings.figures: Budget increase from £166m to £171m; updated cost plan due early 2026; Phase 1 delivers 225 affordable homes
findings.quote: The current development plan at Regina Road is incorporated into the business plan at a delivery cost of £171m for the delivery of Phase 1 including the 225 affordable homes. This is an increase from the reported agreed budget of £166m in the prior year plan... The budget and assumptions remain under review and will be amended as the detailed design evolves and as major contracts are agreed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: Awaab's Law statutory compliance obligations fully unfunded: government allocated £80k nationally, Croydon received £0
findings.detail: New legal obligations require hazard investigation within 10 working days and repairs started within 5 days, with emergency repairs in 24 hours. The government allocated only £80k in 'new burdens' funding; Croydon has received none of this allocation despite identical statutory pressures.
findings.matters: Statutory obligation with tight compliance deadlines carries legal risk if breached; absence of government funding creates unfunded cost pressure on a budget already under strain from covenant breach risk.
findings.figures: Government allocation £80k, Croydon received £0; 10-day investigation, 5-day repair start, 24-hour emergency response requirements
findings.quote: The Government in the muti-year fair funding allocation has included Awaab's law new burdens allocation of only £80k. Croydon has not received any of these funds. Landlords are required to investigate hazards within 10 working days, start fixing within a further 5 working days, and make emergency repairs within 24 hours.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: 630 legacy disrepair cases dating back to 2020 create ongoing compensation liability with no clear end date
findings.detail: The council carries 630 open legal disrepair cases from 2020 onwards requiring both capital remedial works and compensation payments. These cases continue to drain the repairs budget, described as placing 'significant pressure' on it.
findings.matters: This represents a material contingent legal and financial liability; compensation costs are unpredictable and ongoing, creating budget risk that could force operational cuts or trigger further borrowing.
findings.figures: 630 cases from 2020 onwards; placed in 'ongoing' pressure category with no resolution timeline given
findings.quote: 630 legacy disrepair cases from prior years. These cases date back to 2020 and require both remedial works and compensation payments following legal disrepair action. Legacy disrepair cases—along with the associated management and compensation costs—continue to place significant pressure on the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA debt escalates to £860m from £363m baseline, consuming most of the £1,081m debt headroom
findings.detail: The plan requires substantial additional borrowing to fund capital repairs, acquisitions, and the £171m Regina Road regeneration. Debt climbs to £860m by year 30, while annual interest costs rise from £13.5m to £25.5m, leaving limited room for adverse scenarios.
findings.matters: Debt levels and trajectory are fundamental to HRA viability and serviceability; this 2.3x increase in total debt requires sustained strong revenue generation to service.
findings.figures: Opening debt £363m, closing £860m over 30 years; headroom £1,081m; interest costs rise to £25.5m by 2030-31
findings.quote: The opening CFR (Capital Finance Requirement) is £377m of which £363m is funded from borrowing. Additional borrowing will be required to fund both the acquisitions and capital repairs programmes. Debt increases to £860m over the course of the 30 year plan. This is within the projected headroom for the HRA of £1,081m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: Right to Buy policy change eliminates capital receipts, forcing acquisitions to shift to borrowing from 2027-28
findings.detail: Government policy changes in November 2024 restricted RTB discounts, causing applications to collapse from 641 pre-policy to only 28 in the year to November 2025. This eliminates projected capital receipts and forces the acquisitions programme to shift from grants and receipts to debt financing.
findings.matters: RTB receipts were a major financing source; their collapse creates a structural funding gap that must be covered by increased borrowing, compounding the covenant breach risk.
findings.figures: 641 applications pre-policy change, 28 new applications in year to November 2025; borrowing for acquisitions begins 2027-28
findings.quote: Since the implementation of the policy changes there has been a marked reduction in demand with only 28 new applications received in the year to November 2025. The reduced RTB activity has been modelled into the business plan and results in a requirement to support the acquisition programme through borrowing from 2027-28 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - HRA Business Plan and Budget Update 2026-27
findings.headline: Interest cover ratio falls below 1.25 benchmark for 13 years due to required borrowing increases
findings.detail: The recommended ICR ratio of 1.25 is breached as debt increases to fund capital and acquisitions. The ratio stays above 1 but remains below 1.25 through year 13 before recovering, driven by net interest payable rising from £13.5m to £25.5m over five years.
findings.matters: Interest coverage ratio is a key covenant metric for lenders; dropping below 1.25 for an extended period could trigger covenant reviews or constrain future borrowing ability.
findings.figures: Net interest payable £15.4m in 2026-27, rising to £25.5m by 2030-31; ICR below 1.25 but above 1
findings.quote: A minimum ICR (interest rate cover) ratio of 1.25 is recommended. However, the impact of the increased borrowing results in the provisional debt capacity dropping below the benchmark figure but remaining above 1 for the entire plan. The rate recovers by year 13 as operating surpluses are generated.

findings.headline: External auditor issued two Reports in the Public Interest (2020, 2022) citing 'grave governance, operational and financial failures'; improvements are described as 'foundations' of good practice, not resolution.
findings.detail: The council received formal audit reports highlighting 'grave governance, operational and financial failures' and recommendations on capital management. The Capital Strategy is described as a 'continuation of improved capital strategy developed for 2025-26' with 'initial improvements put in place are the foundations of good practice' — language indicating incomplete remediation and ongoing control weakness.
findings.matters: External audit criticism of governance and value-for-money decisions, combined with language suggesting improvements are still foundational, signals governance risk remains material.
findings.figures: Two Reports in the Public Interest published October 2020 and January 2022
findings.quote: The Capital Strategy recognises the complex and challenging financial and operational circumstances in which the Council continues to find itself following two Reports in the Public Interest (RIPI) published by its external auditor (Grant Thornton UK LLP) in October 2020 and January 2022 and subsequent reviews into its financial management arrangements. The reports highlighted grave governance, operational and financial failures within the Council... The Council understands that the initial improvements put in place are the foundations of good practice and is focused on building upon these over the coming months and years.

findings.headline: Asset disposal strategy targeting £200m in receipts, but council acknowledges ability to exceed this is 'dependent on difficult decisions in relation to the future of service delivery.'
findings.detail: The council has identified approximately £200m in potential disposal receipts from surplus property and investment asset sales, essential to minimise debt and running costs. However, the strategy explicitly warns that achieving more than £200m 'will be dependent on difficult decisions in relation to the future of service delivery,' implying either service cuts or major restructuring.
findings.matters: Asset sales are the council's primary lever for reducing debt; the ceiling of £200m is modest relative to £1.8bn total debt, and further sales require service-level decisions the council has not yet made.
findings.figures: £200m potential disposal receipts identified; c.120 council buildings currently occupied
findings.quote: The Council has currently identified approximately £200m of potential disposal receipts based on existing sites previously identified, a review of investment assets and other potential opportunities driven by anticipated service changes. Any ability to achieve receipts in excess of £200m in future years will be dependent on difficult decisions in relation to the future of service delivery, with the overall value of receipts likely limited by previous programmes to rationalise the Council's property portfolio and the market value of potentially surplus assets at any point in time.

findings.headline: Capital programme reduced to 'only essential' works, with continued reliance on capitalisation directions; the council expects conditions to worsen before they improve.
findings.detail: The capital programme has been significantly reduced from pre-2024-25 levels and now comprises only core programmes, statutory obligations, and schemes that deliver cost savings. The strategy explicitly states this 2026-27 programme 'continues on from the 2025-26 Capital Programme in only including essential capital works.' Capitalisation directions (£543.2m over five years) are embedded as assumptions in the medium-term plan, pending government dialogue.
findings.matters: Reduced capital investment signals service deferral; reliance on capitalisation directions is a temporary measure that increases long-term costs and delays the path to sustainability.
findings.figures: £543.2m capitalisation directions assumed 2026-27 to 2030-31 (five-year total); capital programme comprises only 'essential' works
findings.quote: The 2026-27 Capital Strategy continues on from the 2025-26 Capital Programme in only including essential capital works... Capitalisation directions are a significant part of the Capital Programme. These have been included as assumptions in the MTFS in case dialogue with MHCLG does not result in a sustainable financial solution to the historic legacy debt issues and service pressures of the Council. However, it needs to be noted that capitalisation of revenue spend increases the cost of borrowing in following years and is not a solution that would support the Council in becoming financially sustainable.

findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue is 18.5% and rising, when sustainability requires under 10%; HRA ratios also deteriorating.
findings.detail: The General Fund financing cost ratio (debt service costs as a share of revenue) is estimated to rise from 16.5% in 2024-25 to 18.5% in 2026-27 as a result of capitalisation directions and externalisation of internal borrowing. The council acknowledges this is unsustainable and targets under 10%. The Housing Revenue Account ratio is projected to rise from 13.7% to 18.1% by 2028-29.
findings.matters: These ratios are the primary measure of revenue sustainability; ratios this high indicate the council is spending nearly a fifth of revenue on debt service, leaving insufficient funds for service delivery.
findings.quote: The Council estimates that the General Fund financing costs will rise from 16.5% to 18.5% of net revenue owing to the level of capitalisation directions required and the externalisation of internal borrowing. It is acknowledged that the cost of servicing the Council's debt for the General Fund is too high and non-sustainable. A ratio of Financing Costs to the Net Revenue Stream of under 10% should be targeted to ensure sustainability.

findings.headline: Each £100m borrowed through capitalisation directions adds £8.5m per annum to future borrowing costs, and future capital receipts will be insufficient to fund these directions.
findings.detail: Capitalisation directions defer revenue costs into the capital programme (funded over 20 years), increasing the council's long-term debt burden. The council now projects that future capital receipts from asset disposal will be insufficient to fund capitalisation directions, meaning General Fund annual borrowing costs are projected to be £86m in 2026-27 — a structural shift from prior years when asset sales could offset the cost impact.
findings.matters: This indicates the council is trapped in a cycle where asset sales no longer offset the cost of capitalisation; future interest costs will continue to grow even as the council shrinks its property footprint.
findings.figures: Each £100m capitalisation direction = £8.5m per annum additional borrowing cost; General Fund annual borrowing costs projected at £86m in 2026-27
findings.quote: Each additional £100m borrowed through capitalisation directions would add an estimated £8.5m per annum to future borrowing costs. In recent years, capital receipts from the Asset Disposal Strategy have been used to fund capitalisation directions and, therefore, the Council was not able to reduce its existing historic debt (a situation of 'treading water'). The future capital receipts will be insufficient to fund capitalisation directions, so General Fund annual borrowing costs are projected to be £86m in 2026-27.

findings.headline: The council cannot achieve financial sustainability without further government assistance and faces a budget gap of £119m for 2026-27.
findings.detail: The council has formally concluded that expenditure anticipated in each year of 2026-30 will exceed available financial resources, and that reaching financial and operational sustainability without additional Government assistance is not possible. The 2025-26 budget required £136m in capitalisation directions from Government to balance; the Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows an estimated budget gap of £119m for 2026-27 alone.
findings.matters: This signals ongoing revenue sustainability issues and continued dependence on government bailouts rather than structural budget balance.
findings.figures: £136m capitalisation directions required to balance 2025-26 budget; £119m estimated budget gap for 2026-27
findings.quote: The Council has concluded that the expenditure it is anticipated to incur in each year of the period 2026-30 is likely to exceed the financial resources available and that reaching financial and operational sustainability without further Government assistance will not be possible. The Council's 2025-26 budget required capitalisation directions from Government of £136m to balance and the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) demonstrates an estimated budget gap of £119m for 2026-27 (owing to historic debt costs and the service pressures that have emerged nationally, regionally and locally).

findings.headline: Between 2017-18 and 2019-20 the council borrowed £545m with no focused debt management plan, leaving it exposed to refinancing risk at higher rates.
findings.detail: In a three-year period, the council accumulated £545m in borrowing without a structured debt management strategy. The majority of this debt comprises short-term borrowings rather than long-term fixed instruments, leaving the council severely exposed to interest rate risk as these loans come due for refinancing in a higher rate environment.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing that rolls over at higher rates will add substantial cost pressure to the revenue budget and undermines financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £545m borrowed 2017-18 to 2019-20; majority held as short-term borrowings
findings.quote: In the three years between 2017-18 and 2019-20 the Council borrowed £545m with no focused debt management plan in place. The majority of this debt comprises short-term borrowings which has left the Council exposed to current higher interest rates and, therefore, driving significant increases in annual borrowing costs.

findings.headline: General Fund debt of £1.388bn represents 16% of core spending power in annual servicing costs alone.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund debt (excluding IFRS16 accounting adjustments) stands at £1.388bn, with a total debt burden of £1.8bn including Housing Revenue Account debt. Over £70m per annum is required to service this debt, consuming circa 16% of the Council's core spending power. The council incurred £300m of this debt investing in assets which have not retained their value, leaving debt exceeding asset value.
findings.matters: This level of debt service consumes a critical share of available revenue, leaving less for service delivery and making the council dependent on asset sales and government support.
findings.figures: £1.388bn General Fund debt (excluding £0.070bn IFRS16 adjustment); £1.8bn total debt burden including £0.4bn HRA debt; £70m annual debt service (~16% of core spending power); £300m borrowed for assets that did not hold value
findings.quote: With £1.388bn of General Fund debt (excluding the IFRS16 leases technical accounting adjustment of an extra £0.070bn) and an environment of higher interest rates the continued delivery of an effective Asset Management Plan and an ambitious Asset Disposal Strategy, including reducing the number of buildings used by the Council, is essential to mitigate rising cost pressures, minimise increases in the overall debt burden and help the Council balance its books.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: The council holds £90.6m in short-term investments but deems it necessary to hold £75–100m for day-to-day operations, leaving almost no buffer.
findings.detail: The council's liquid investment holdings are almost entirely committed to operational needs. Any unexpected shortfall in income or acceleration of spending will require either drawdown of reserves earmarked for other purposes or emergency borrowing. The council currently holds exactly the minimum it judges necessary to operate.
findings.matters: A lender sees no financial cushion; a finance director has no discretionary funds for savings delivery or slippage.
findings.figures: Current Treasury investments: £90.6m (31/12/25). Required liquid holdings: £75–100m. Residual net investment income budgeted for 2026/27: £1.5m.
findings.quote: The Council deems it appropriate to hold between £75-100m in liquid investments in order to ensure it has the funds to meet its day to day expenditure arising from its operating needs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: The HRA (housing) financing cost to revenue ratio is rising to 18.1% by 2028/29, while the HRA debt-to-revenues ratio deteriorates to 4.4.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is self-contained but is deteriorating. HRA debt servicing costs are projected to eat up 18.1% of HRA revenue by 2028/29 (from 13.7% in 2024/25). The HRA 30-year business plan shows significant additional borrowing will be required 'over the next few years and then debt will need to be refinanced in future years. This extra borrowing must be self-financed from the HRA account.' There is no mention of where this refinancing will come from.
findings.matters: A lender sees a self-contained housing fund that is becoming unaffordable; a finance director faces pressure to raise rents or cut maintenance to service debt.
findings.figures: HRA cost of debt to revenue: 13.7% (2024/25 actual) rising to 18.1% (2028/29 estimate). HRA debt to revenues: 4.4 (2028/29). HRA capital expenditure 2026/27: £101.1m, with only £26.5m from HRA revenue.
findings.quote: This extra borrowing must be self-financed from the HRA account.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: The Capital Financing Requirement is projected to grow from £1.8bn to £2.3bn over four years, with no credible plan to reduce it.
findings.detail: The CFR—the measure of the council's total indebtedness—is rising by £493m between 2024/25 and 2028/29. This is driven by capital spending (much funded by Capitalisation Directions and capital grants) and the addition of £70.2m of lease liabilities under IFRS 16. The Liability Benchmark chart shows the council will need to increase external borrowing significantly; from 2025 to 2047, 'new loans and refinancing will be required to meet the borrowing requirement as the Existing Loans Outstanding are below the LB line.'
findings.matters: A lender sees a council whose debt burden is structurally rising and will not stabilise for 20 years; a finance director has no headroom to slow capital spending without government permission.
findings.figures: CFR: £1,834.9m (31/03/25 actual) rising to £2,328.1m (31/03/29 estimate). IFRS 16 adjustment: £70.2m. HRA debt to revenues ratio: 4.4 by 2028/29 (from 3.6 current).
findings.quote: The LB for the General Fund shows that from 2025 to 2047 new loans and refinancing will be required to meet the borrowing requirement as the Existing Loans Outstanding are below the LB line.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: The council must refinance and raise new borrowing totalling approximately £478m in the next 12 months while interest rates remain elevated.
findings.detail: £278m of existing debt matures in the next 12 months (18.4% of the total borrowing portfolio). On top of this, the council needs new borrowing of approximately £200m to fund the capital programme. The council must do this while PWLB 5-year rates are at 4.81% and 10-year rates at 5.39%. The strategy is to 'spread the refinancing of maturing debt and new borrowing over a short to medium term period' to try to align with MRP, but there is no guarantee rates will fall.
findings.matters: A lender faces rollover risk if rates do not fall as forecast; a finance director faces certainty of higher interest costs if rates stay flat.
findings.figures: Maturing debt (next 12 months): £278.0m. New borrowing requirement: ~£200m. 5-year PWLB rate: 4.81% (22 Dec 2025). 10-year PWLB rate: 5.39%.
findings.quote: Over the course of the next calendar year the Council will need to refinance £278m of maturing debt and require new borrowing in the region of £200m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: The council's perceived credit quality is 'very low', leaving it with only the Public Works Loan Board as a viable borrower.
findings.detail: No commercial lender will touch Croydon at any price. The council can only borrow from the government-backed PWLB. This is not a choice: it is a forced outcome of the council's financial history, including 'legacy debt issues associated with unsuccessful commercial investments'. The PWLB Certainty Rate for general fund borrowing is gilts +80 basis points; the council pays a 20bp premium over smaller authorities.
findings.matters: A lender sees a council locked out of market funding and entirely dependent on government goodwill; a finance director has zero flexibility to refinance at better terms.
findings.figures: PWLB Certainty Rate: gilts +80 bps for General Fund, gilts +40 bps for HRA (as at 22 December 2025). Current 5-year PWLB borrowing rate: 4.81%.
findings.quote: Due to the Council's continuing need for exceptional financial support from the Government the perceived credit quality of the Council is very low, so the only viable source of borrowing will continue to be from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) where funds can be borrowed for up to 50 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: The council has deliberately under-borrowed by £160–207m, using cash reserves to cover the gap between capital needs and borrowed funds.
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement (what the council needs to borrow) exceeds actual external debt by £206.5m by 2026/27. This is not accidental: the council is using reserves and cash balances as a temporary funding source rather than borrowing, in the hope that interest rates fall. This strategy leaves the council with minimal liquidity for shocks and forces it to refinance £278m of debt in the next 12 months while simultaneously drawing down reserves.
findings.matters: A lender sees a council betting on falling rates; if rates stay flat or rise, the council will be forced to refinance at unfavourable rates. A finance director has almost no buffer for unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Under/over borrowing: £160.8m (2024/25 actual), £206.5m (2025/26 forecast through 2028/29). Debt maturing within 12 months: £278.0m (18.4% of total borrowing portfolio at 31/12/25).
findings.quote: The Authority continues to maintain an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: Financing costs are 16–18% of the council's net revenue, acknowledged in the paper as unsustainable and unaffordable in the long term.
findings.detail: The council's debt servicing cost as a proportion of net revenue spending is 16.5% (actual 2024/25), forecast to rise to 18.2% (2025/26). The paper explicitly states this level is 'too high and not sustainable in the long term' and that ratios of under 10% should be targeted. The HRA financing cost ratio is projected to reach 18.1% by 2028/29. These are among the worst borrowing cost ratios in English local government.
findings.matters: A lender is exposed to a council that cannot service its debt from operations and is entirely dependent on government bailout; a finance director faces the certainty of spending cuts in services if rates rise or support ends.
findings.figures: General Fund financing cost to net revenue stream: 16.5% (2024/25 actual), 18.2% (2025/26 forecast), 17.7% (2026/27 estimate). HRA cost of debt to revenue: 13.7% (2024/25), projected 18.1% (2028/29). Target ratio should be under 10%.
findings.quote: It is acknowledged that the cost of servicing the Council's debt for the General Fund is too high and not sustainable in the long term and a ratio of Financing Costs to the Net Revenue Stream of under 10% should be targeted to ensure sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement MRP Policy Statement and Annual Invest
findings.headline: Council depends on exceptional government financial support to balance its budget and mitigate a structural deficit.
findings.detail: Croydon cannot operate as a self-sustaining council and requires ongoing central government intervention through Capitalisation Directions. The council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy and budget reports depend entirely on this support. This is not a temporary measure but a permanent feature of the council's financial model.
findings.matters: A lender faces existential risk if government support changes, and a finance director has zero room for unexpected shocks.
findings.figures: £119.1m of the £220.2m General Fund capital expenditure planned for 2026/27 is funded by Capitalisation Directions.
findings.quote: The Council remains significantly dependent on exceptional financial support from central Government to mitigate its structural budget deficit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: No updated financial strategy yet; demand management and growth control deferred to later years
findings.detail: The S151 officer states that 'more work needs to be done' to develop a financial strategy showing effective demand management across major pressure points. 2026-27 is described as 'transitional', with hopes to reduce growth figures in later years.
findings.matters: The absence of an updated financial strategy demonstrates the council is in reactive mode with unconstrained growth estimates and no clear plan to address underlying demand pressures.
findings.figures: Major pressures: children's services £6.6m, adults' services £7.3m, temporary accommodation £4.8m
findings.quote: More work needs to be done as part of developing a new financial strategy to show that the Council has effective demand management strategies in place across its major financial pressure points and that it intervenes and commissions effectively to tackle instances of market failure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: New Section 151 Officer in post since January 2026, relying on longer-serving staff
findings.detail: The current S151 Officer (Corporate Director of Resources) has been in post for only 8 months (since 5 January 2026). The statement relies significantly on advice from longer-serving officers, and the S151 officer deferred making major adjustments to draft figures prepared in November.
findings.matters: A recently appointed S151 Officer in a council under Commissioners introduces uncertainty about continuity of financial strategy and the robustness of this statement.
findings.figures: Appointed 5 January 2026
findings.quote: I have been in this role since 5 January 2026 and so in writing this statement I have relied on advice from longer-serving officers within the finance division and across the authority.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: Future Croydon transformation programme risks £8.2m savings target; £5m contingency held
findings.detail: The transformation programme targets £8.2m in 2026-27 savings across complex projects including digital tools and management restructuring. A £5m contingency budget is held specifically to mitigate non-delivery risk. The S151 officer flags this as 'perhaps above all others' the key risk to manage closely.
findings.matters: A £5m hedge against £8.2m planned savings (61% coverage) indicates material delivery uncertainty. Failure to deliver would force mid-year budget adjustments.
findings.figures: £8.2m target savings, £5m risk contingency
findings.quote: The 'Future Croydon' transformation programme is targeted to deliver Target Operating Model (TOM) related savings of £8.2m in 2026/27... A risk contingency budget of £5m is held in corporate to mitigate risks relating to non-delivery of savings... it is appropriate to highlight this area perhaps above all others as a key risk to be managed closely during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: Government Commissioners challenge growth estimates as potentially overstated
findings.detail: The appointed Commissioners have consistently expressed concern that the council's total growth figures (£56m) may be higher than strictly necessary. The S151 officer agrees reducing these figures will be essential for medium-term planning.
findings.matters: Commissioners' view suggests the council's demand forecasting may be inaccurate or that unconstrained growth masks the absence of effective demand management.
findings.figures: Total growth £56m (£23m inflation, £33m service pressures)
findings.quote: Croydon has Commissioners appointed by MHCLG. They have expressed a consistent view that the growth figures may be higher than strictly necessary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: Council under Government Commissioners and relying on Exceptional Financial Support to set budget
findings.detail: MHCLG has appointed Commissioners to oversee Croydon's financial position. The council cannot balance its 2026-27 budget through normal means and is using Government agreed Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: External intervention and reliance on exceptional support indicates the council is in financial distress and unable to self-manage its budget position.
findings.figures: Commissioners appointed; Exceptional Financial Support scheme active
findings.quote: The Council is in continuous contact with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), including through the Government's appointed Commissioners, about its financial position and is currently using Government agreed Exceptional Financial Support to set its budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: Council non-compliant with Prudential Code due to disproportionately high General Fund debt
findings.detail: Croydon does not comply with all aspects of the Prudential Code for Capital Finance. This is attributed to the council's unusually high level of General Fund debt relative to prudent practice.
findings.matters: Prudential Code non-compliance signals the council's borrowing position is materially out of line with safe practice and reflects constrained financial flexibility.
findings.figures: General Fund debt described as 'disproportionately high'
findings.quote: However, owing to the Council's disproportionately high level of General Fund debt it is not compliant with all aspects of the Prudential Code.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4F - 2026-27 Section 25 Statement by the Corporate Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)
findings.headline: SEND overspend restated upward to £16.7m from £4.7m, triggering CIPFA review
findings.detail: The Special Educational Needs and Disabilities deficit within the Dedicated Schools Grant has been revised up by over £12m. This restatement prompted a CIPFA review of SEND placements recording, payments and forecasting, indicating material issues in how the DSG has been managed and accounted for.
findings.matters: A £16.7m unplanned overspend on a statutory service signals control failures in forecast accuracy and financial management on a major budget line.
findings.figures: £16.7m (increased from £4.7m)
findings.quote: The overspend on Special Educational Needs and disabilities (SEND) in 2024-25 has now increased to £16.7m from the £4.7m reported in the provisional outturn report.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant DSG Deficit Management Plan Outturn 2024-25- Final
findings.headline: The £28.1m DSG deficit is ring-fenced from General Fund only by statutory override ending 2025-26 (extended to 2027-28 but not yet legislated); council has no plan to use its own resources to cover it
findings.detail: Under the statutory override, the DSG deficit 'must not be charged to a General Fund but must be charged to a separate fund' and is 'disregarded in terms of the LA's financial sustainability'. The override runs to end of 2025-26 and has been extended to March 2028 'but the Government has committed to extending this to March 2028. This has yet to be legislated for.' The council explicitly states it 'does not intend to seek to commit any cash injection from its General Fund budget to offset some of the overall DSG deficit' because of 'the Council's current financial position and ongoing budgetary constraints'.
findings.matters: Without the override, a £28.1m+ deficit would immediately consume reserves or force the council into a negative General Fund position. The override is temporary and not yet legislated. The council cannot self-fund any remediation.
findings.figures: £28.1m net DSG deficit at 31/3/25; statutory override to 2025-26 (extended to 2027-28); £38.0m adjustment account deficit plus £9.9m reserve
findings.quote: The risk relating to the DSG deficit impact on the General Fund is currently mitigated through the statutory override up to the end of 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant DSG Deficit Management Plan Outturn 2024-25- Final
findings.headline: Safety Valve programme closes 1 April 2026 and is replaced by High Needs Stability Grant (£35-40m) that is conditional, delayed, and only paid after approval of a SEND reform plan
findings.detail: Croydon received £10.960m (2022-23), £4.480m (2023-24) and £2.100m (2024-25) under Safety Valve. The programme ends 31 March 2026. The replacement High Needs Stability Grant of estimated '£35m to £40m' will be 'paid in Autumn 2026', six months later. The grant is only paid 'once a local authority has developed and submitted to the Department for Education a Local SEND reform plan which is then approved'. The Secretary of State 'may reduce, suspend or withhold grant payments or require the repayment' if the council fails to comply with grant conditions. DfE will scrutinise for 'ineligible spend' including 'charges relating to Equal Pay claims' and will use the 'lowest total DSG deficit figure' if accounts differ.
findings.matters: The £27.4m five-year Safety Valve support ends. The replacement funding is smaller, delayed by months, conditional on an uncertain approval, and subject to clawback. There is a funding cliff in April 2026 and June 2026 gap before replacement payment.
findings.figures: Safety Valve £27.4m over 5 years; replacement grant £35-40m estimated; paid Autumn 2026 (six months after SV ends)
findings.quote: Initial estimates suggest the grant could be in the range of £35m to £40m, relating to a contribution to write off the majority of the deficit as at 31/3/26, and will be paid in Autumn 2026.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant DSG Deficit Management Plan Outturn 2024-25- Final
findings.headline: Final 2024-25 DSG overspend jumped from £4.7m provisional to £16.7m after accruals review, signalling material weakness in financial control
findings.detail: The provisional outturn reported £4.7m overspend but the final figure was £16.7m — an understatement of £12m — 'following completion of work to calculate and review accruals required for SEND placements'. Separately, IT system migration 'did not have direct integration with the finance system', creating 'discrepancies in the financial records' and delays. The council commissioned CIPFA to review SEND placement recording and forecasting; the review is 'currently being finalised'.
findings.matters: A £12m restatement mid-year undermines confidence in the forward forecasts and budget monitoring discipline. The IT issues and reliance on an external review to fix them suggest systemic weakness.
findings.figures: £16.7m final overspend vs £4.7m provisional (£12.0m variance); 2024-25 undisclosed but multiple undisclosed system issues
findings.quote: The final 2024-25 DSG in-year overspend was £16.7m, increased from the £4.7m reported in the provisional outturn report, following completion of work to calculate and review accruals required for SEND placements.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant DSG Deficit Management Plan Outturn 2024-25- Final
findings.headline: EHCP numbers have risen to 6,000 (up 675 in one year) and local provision has not kept pace, forcing continued reliance on costly out-of-borough and independent placements
findings.detail: The council created 137 new special school placements and six new Enhanced Learning Provisions but demand continues to outpace supply. The borough is 'compelled to seek out-of-borough placements to meet needs'. The percentage attending non-maintained independent special schools 'has remained fairly static (8%) but the numbers have increased'. Reception-aged children requiring specialist placement 'had a significant impact on the budget that was forecast for 2024-25'.
findings.matters: This shows the financial problem is structural. The council cannot build local capacity fast enough to arrest cost growth.
findings.figures: EHCP numbers 6,000 (increase of 675 from 2023-24); 137 new special school placements created in 2024-25; 6 new ELPs opened in 2024-25; 7 new ELPs proposed for 2025-26
findings.quote: There has been a continued increase in the number of EHCPs in Croydon, rising to 6,000 (an increase of 675 from the 2023-24 academic year).

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant DSG Deficit Management Plan Outturn 2024-25- Final
findings.headline: Special school and independent placement costs have increased 69% and 72% over two years, driven by provider fee increases of 20%+ that are outside council control
findings.detail: Spend on special schools rose 69% and independent special schools 72% from 2022-23 to 2024-25, with the increase 'driven mainly by the unit cost of placements rather than activity levels'. Independent schools are demanding fee uplifts 'of upwards of 20% from the year before'. One academy special school took no year 7 pupils and the council had to find external places 'at very high costs'.
findings.matters: This is the primary cost driver and it is not demand-driven but cost-driven, making it harder for the council to manage. Provider behaviour is pricing the council out.
findings.figures: 69% increase in special schools spend, 72% increase in independent special schools spend 2022-23 to 2024-25
findings.quote: Table 2 below shows an overall increase in special schools and independent special schools' costs of 69% and 72% respectively from the 2022-23 position. This is driven mainly by the unit cost of placements rather than activity levels.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant DSG Deficit Management Plan Outturn 2024-25- Final
findings.headline: Council is forecasting £19.0m in-year DSG overspend for 2025-26, off the Safety Valve target of £0.113m balance and signalling structural failure of the deficit control plan
findings.detail: The Safety Valve agreement required Croydon to reach in-year balance by end-2025-26. Instead it is forecasting £19.0m overspend (£20m high needs less £1m early years underspend). The council has 'not met the Safety Valve targets' in 2024-25 or 2025-26. The cumulative position is worsening: deficit forecast to grow from £28.1m at 31/3/25 to £43.9m at 31/3/26 before the replacement grant is applied.
findings.matters: This shows the council's five-year deficit management plan is failing at its core objective. The underlying SEND demand problem (EHCP numbers up 675 in one year) is not being solved.
findings.figures: £19.0m overspend forecast for 2025-26; £28.1m net DSG deficit at 31/3/25; variance from DfE forecast of £38.4m worse than expected
findings.quote: In 2025-26, the LA is forecasting an in-year overspend of £19.0m for the DSG (£20.0m overspend for the high needs block less £1m underspend for the early years block).

findings.headline: Net pension liability of £90.7 million with significant valuation uncertainty
findings.detail: The authority's net defined benefit pension liability is £90.7 million on the balance sheet and is identified as a key audit matter due to its size and sensitivity to actuarial assumptions such as contribution rates, benefit increases, fund growth rates and longevity.
findings.matters: A £90.7m pension obligation represents a significant future liability. Given the authority's financial crisis and minimal reserves, underfunding of pension obligations creates additional long-term liability.
findings.figures: £90.7 million net defined benefit liability
findings.quote: The Authority's pension fund net liability, as reflected in its Balance Sheet as the net defined benefit liability, represents a significant estimate in the financial statements. The pension fund net liability is considered a significant estimate due to the size of the numbers involved (£90.7 million in the Authority Balance Sheet)

findings.headline: Low general fund reserves and in-year budget overspends create fraud risk due to pressure to deliver balanced budget
findings.detail: Auditors identified presumed risk of fraud in expenditure recognition, citing pressure to deliver balanced budget, low general fund reserves, and in-year budget overspends as creating significant risk that operating expenditure and creditor balances may be incomplete.
findings.matters: Low reserves combined with budget overspends indicates financial strain and creates conditions where management might manipulate accounts to show compliance. This is a material fraud risk in the audit.
findings.figures: Specific reserve level unquantified; in-year overspends amount unspecified
findings.quote: Due to the pressure to deliver a balanced budget, the low level of General Fund reserves held by the Authority and in-year budget overspends there is a significant risk over the completeness of the operating expenditure and associated creditor balances.

findings.headline: Six consecutive years of audit disclaimers from 2020 through 2025
findings.detail: On 13 December 2024, auditors issued disclaimers on financial statements for years ended 31 March 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024. The current year (2025) adds a sixth consecutive year without any clean audit opinion. This pattern indicates chronic and systemic inability to produce auditable financial statements.
findings.matters: Six consecutive years of audit failure without clean opinion is exceptional and indicates deep institutional governance and financial reporting problems that cannot be dismissed as one-off issues.
findings.quote: On 13 December 2024 we issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements for the years ended 31 March 2020, 31 March 2021, 31 March 2022, 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024.

findings.headline: Government appointed commissioners implemented due to unsustainable debt burden and continued reliance on government financial support
findings.detail: On 6 October 2025, auditors made a formal written recommendation regarding the council's continued reliance on government financial support and unsustainable debt burden. A government appointed commissioner-led model has been implemented. This is classified as a significant weakness in the authority's value-for-money arrangements.
findings.matters: Government-appointed commissioner intervention is the most extreme governance step available and indicates the council is in financial crisis and unable to manage independently. This is the ultimate red flag for any lender considering lending to this authority.
findings.figures: Commissioner-led intervention implemented October 2025
findings.quote: On 6 October 2025 we made a written recommendation to the Authority under section 24 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014. This was in relation the Authority's continued reliance on government financial support, resulting in an unsustainable debt burden and a government appointed commissioner led model being implemented.

findings.headline: £137.2 million in MHCLG capitalisation entries lack sufficient audit evidence
findings.detail: The financial statements include £137.2 million in accounting entries from MHCLG capitalisation directives credited to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement and Movement in Reserves Statement. The auditors were unable to obtain sufficient evidence over this balance and its potential impact on previous periods. This matter alone would have modified the audit opinion if a disclaimer had not been issued.
findings.matters: £137.2 million represents a material amount that cannot be properly verified, making it impossible to confirm the authority's true financial position or the accuracy of prior years' accounts.
findings.figures: £137.2 million
findings.quote: While MHCLG have confirmed that the Authority is permitted to include these values in the CIES and MIRS, we were unable to obtain sufficient, appropriate evidence over this balance and the potential impact on the financial statements for the previous periods.

findings.headline: £62.6 million Fairfield Halls refurbishment linked to governance failures and police investigation for misconduct in public office
findings.detail: The auditors reference their January 2022 public interest report on the Fairfield Halls refurbishment by the council's subsidiary Brick by Brick Croydon Ltd. This identified potential non-compliance with laws and regulations. A forensic investigation was commissioned, and management referred matters to the Metropolitan Police to consider whether a misconduct in public office offence has been committed.
findings.matters: A £62.6m scheme with active police investigation for potential criminal misconduct by officers indicates serious governance failures and legal liability that create material risk for creditors and the authority.
findings.figures: £62.6 million
findings.quote: The £62.6 million refurbishment of Fairfield Halls was undertaken by the Authority's wholly owned subsidiary Brick by Brick Croydon Ltd and funded by the Authority. This report highlighted potential non-compliance with laws and regulations by the Authority.

findings.headline: Auditors have disclaimed opinion on the entire set of financial statements for 2024-25
findings.detail: Grant Thornton has issued a disclaimer of opinion rather than any audit opinion on Croydon's accounts. They state they were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the backstop date to conclude the financial statements are free from material misstatement. This means it is impossible to verify whether the accounts are accurate.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion is the worst possible audit outcome and means the auditor cannot confirm the financial statements are reliable, which is critical for lenders assessing creditworthiness and for the council's finance director.
findings.figures: Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the backstop date to conclude that the Authority's and group's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 as a whole are free from material misstatement.

findings.headline: Pension net liability highly sensitive to actuarial assumptions; 0.1% change in discount rate = 2% impact on £90.678m liability
findings.detail: The Council's net defined benefit pension liability is £90.678m. The estimate is highly sensitive to key assumptions (discount rate, inflation rate, salary increase, life expectancy). A 0.1% change in discount and inflation rates produces approximately a 2% effect on the liability. The auditor concluded there is a significant risk of material misstatement in the IAS 19 estimate due to the assumptions used, though no assurance issues were identified in the actuary's work.
findings.matters: The pension liability is a material component of the council's balance sheet. High sensitivity to interest rate assumptions means small changes in economic conditions could materially affect reported liabilities. Lenders need to understand this volatility.
findings.figures: Net pension liability: £90.678m. Sensitivity: 0.1% change in discount/inflation rates = ~2% impact on liability.
findings.quote: A small change in the key assumptions (discount rate, inflation rate, salary increase and life expectancy) can have a significant impact on the estimated IAS 19 liability... a 0.1% change in these two assumptions would have approximately 2% effect on the liability/asset.

findings.headline: Net £9.7m adjustment to Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement from audit work
findings.detail: The auditor identified adjustments totalling a net £9.7m to the Council's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. These include the High Needs Block adjustment, revenue reclassifications, and other items identified during testing. The adjustment represents material misstatements corrected during the audit.
findings.matters: A £9.7m adjustment indicates the draft accounts were materially misstated before audit corrections. For a council under financial stress, material restatements undermine credibility with lenders and regulators.
findings.figures: Net £9.7m adjustment to Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement.
findings.quote: We have a number of adjustments to the financial statements with the Council, resulting in a net £9.7m adjustment to the Council's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting incomplete; lease liabilities and right-of-use assets not fully recognized on balance sheet
findings.detail: IFRS 16 (leases) implementation has resulted in incomplete disclosures. The Council's lease liabilities and corresponding right-of-use assets are not being recognised on the balance sheet, giving rise to an understatement of both assets and liabilities. When draft financial statements were published, IFRS 16 detail was not included as the Council made significant attempts to obtain information for full disclosures, but work remained incomplete.
findings.matters: Understating both assets and liabilities distorts the council's reported financial position. Lenders need accurate information on the full scope of lease obligations to assess debt capacity and sustainability.
findings.figures: Lease liabilities and right-of-use assets: amount understated not specified in document.
findings.quote: The absence of the entries required by this standard results in the Council's lease liabilities and corresponding right-of-use assets not being recognised, giving rise to an understatement of both assets and liabilities in the Balance Sheet.

findings.headline: Creditor and debtor balances lack supporting documentation: £2.563m creditors and £1.2m debtors unverified
findings.detail: During detailed testing of creditor items, the Council was unable to provide supporting documentation for £2.563m of creditor balances (23 items still subject to query, 25 awaiting evidence with no further work performed due to disclaimed opinion). Similarly, supporting documentation for £1.2m of debtor balances could not be provided. Additionally, 31 debtor items were still subject to query and 17 awaited evidence.
findings.matters: An inability to document nearly £4m in payables and receivables indicates serious control and record-keeping failures. This undermines confidence in the completeness and accuracy of the balance sheet and suggests potential unrecognized liabilities.
findings.figures: £2.563m of creditor balances undocumented. £1.2m of debtor balances undocumented. 31 debtor items in query; 17 awaiting evidence; 23 creditor items in query; 25 creditors awaiting evidence.
findings.quote: the Council was unable to provide supporting documentation for £2.563 million of creditor balances. Additionally, the Council was unable to provide supporting documentation for £1.2 million of debtor balances.

findings.headline: £1.8m cash in transit understatement from housing rent system; supporting evidence unavailable
findings.detail: The cash in transit balance in the cashbook is understated by approximately £1.8m relating to transactions within the Council's housing rent system. The Council could not provide supporting evidence for these transactions. Following discussions, the Council agreed the balance should either be reclassified as a debtor or written back to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement as an expense. The discrepancy affects the reported bank overdraft balance on the balance sheet.
findings.matters: A £1.8m unexplained item in cash, combined with inability to provide evidence, signals control weaknesses in the housing system and raises questions about what else may not be properly documented. It directly affects the reported cash position.
findings.figures: £1.8m understatement in cash in transit balance.
findings.quote: the cash in transit balance recorded in the cashbook is understated by approximately £1.8m. This amount relates to transactions within the Council's housing rent system, for which supporting evidence could not be provided.

findings.headline: Fixed Asset Register not updated for valuations 2020-21 through 2023-24, creating material depreciation risk
findings.detail: Management had not updated the Fixed Asset Register for valuations from prior years covering 2020-21 through 2023-24. This creates a risk of material errors because asset movements and associated depreciation calculations are based on incorrect data. It represents non-compliance with CIPFA code and accounting standards. The auditor could not complete property, plant and equipment audit procedures as a result.
findings.matters: A four-year backlog in updating the asset register means depreciation charges and asset valuations in the accounts may be materially wrong. Lenders need confidence in the value of council assets and the sustainability of their financial position.
findings.figures: Four-year backlog: 2020-21 through 2023-24 valuations not reflected in Fixed Asset Register.
findings.quote: management had not updated the Fixed Asset Register (FAR) for the valuations from prior years (2020/21 through to 2023/24). This creates a risk of material errors in the financial statements, as assets movements and the associated calculated depreciation would be based on incorrect data.

findings.headline: Revenue recognition errors: £2.363m misclassified and £6.7m potential cut-off error in fees and charges
findings.detail: Testing of fees and charges identified a £2.363m reclassification (income incorrectly recorded as fees and charges instead of grants and contributions, adjusted in the final accounts). Additionally, testing identified £63k of income earned in 2023-24 incorrectly recognised in 2024-25. Extrapolation of this cut-off error indicates a potential population error of £6.7m. Supporting documentation was challenging to obtain and of inconsistent quality.
findings.matters: Revenue errors directly affect reported position. A £6.7m potential error that was not fully investigated due to backstop limitations means the revenue position may be understated by a material amount. The pattern suggests systemic cut-off and documentation issues.
findings.figures: £2.363m reclassification (adjusted). £63k identified cut-off error. Extrapolated potential error: £6.7m.
findings.quote: testing identified £63k in respect of income earned in 2023/24 which had been incorrectly recognised in 2024/25. Extrapolation of this error across the population indicates a potential error, should it be repeated across the whole population, of £6.7m.

findings.headline: High Needs Block expenditure overstated by £15.6m due to data quality and system failures
findings.detail: During the audit, the Council identified issues with High Needs Block expenditure valuation. Contributing factors included data quality issues and system limitations, with difficulties matching invoices to purchase orders. The final creditor position moved significantly, resulting in an overspend of £19.1m (previously reported as £3.5m). Management adjusted the financial statements for £15.6m of error, including £2.4m attributable to prior years.
findings.matters: A £15.6m misstatement in SEND costs is material and indicates fundamental system and control failures in the Council's expenditure tracking. The revision from £3.5m to £19.1m overspend suggests deep visibility problems in the most complex budget area.
findings.figures: £19.1m High Needs Block overspend (revised from £3.5m). £15.6m adjustment made. £2.4m relating to prior years.
findings.quote: Following the review, the final High Needs Block creditor position has moved significantly, resulting in an overspend of £19.1m (previously £3.5m) giving rise to a misstatement of £15.6m in the 2024/25 value of SEND costs, including £2.4m attributable to years before 2024-25.

findings.headline: Unsustainable debt burden requires government-appointed commissioner-led intervention
findings.detail: The auditor identified a significant weakness in the Authority's financial sustainability arrangements and issued a statutory recommendation. The finding centres on continued reliance on government financial support resulting in an unsustainable debt burden, which has triggered the implementation of a government-appointed commissioner-led model of governance.
findings.matters: A government-appointed commissioner replaces normal council decision-making on finances. This is a direct signal to lenders that the council cannot manage its own finances and is now under external control. It is a material credit event.
findings.figures: Pension liability alone: £90.678m net defined benefit liability. Statutory recommendation issued.
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. In addition, as part of our review, we identified that the significant weakness in the Council's financial sustainability arrangements was such that we issued a statutory recommendation. This relating to continued reliance on government financial support, resulting in an unsustainable debt burden and a government appointed commissioner led model being implemented.

findings.headline: Audit opinion disclaimed; backstop deadline means assurance on opening balances cannot be obtained
findings.detail: The auditor cannot issue an unmodified opinion because prior years' audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed opinions. Without assurance over opening balances and with incomplete work on depreciation, debtors, and creditors, the auditor anticipates a disclaimed opinion. The Council has demonstrated positive efforts, but the 27 February 2026 backstop deadline means the audit work cannot be completed to full standard.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means lenders and the finance director have no third-party assurance on the accuracy of the financial statements. This is a material governance risk and directly affects credit decisions.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 27 February 2026. Prior opinions: disclaimed due to backstop requirements.
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where prior years' audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed opinions, we have been unable to perform sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.headline: Social rent convergence postponed, removing a planned additional income source scheduled for April 2027.
findings.detail: The government's 10-year rent settlement originally included a convergence mechanism allowing additional rent increases (£1/week from April 2027, rising to £2/week) to bring social rents to formula rent levels. The Autumn 2025 Budget announced this convergence would not proceed immediately, with full implementation details deferred to January 2026. If the HRA business plan incorporated convergence income projections from 2027 onwards, this postponement removes a material revenue stream.
findings.matters: The HRA may have modelled future rent increases and capital investment based on convergence income. A postponement could create a budget gap starting in 2027-28 unless alternative funding is identified.
findings.figures: Convergence was to add £1/week from April 2027, rising to £2/week until full convergence achieved
findings.quote: As part of the Autumn 2025 Budget, the Chancellor has announced that the planned implementation of social rent convergence will not proceed immediately as originally intended. A pause was announced on the planned convergence of social rents, with the full implementation scheme to be set out in January 2026.

findings.headline: 31% of tenants receive no housing benefits and face unmitigated rent increases.
findings.detail: Croydon's HRA includes 31.06% of tenants receiving no housing benefits or universal credit. These self-payers face the full impact of 4.8% rent increases with no automatic support. The council's hardship fund, which historically supported 119 residents with £59,500, requires fresh Secretary of State approval each year and cannot be relied upon as permanent mitigation. Demand in the first half of 2025-26 (61 residents, £30,500) suggests annual demand of approximately £61,000.
findings.matters: Unaffordable rents create tenant arrears and bad debt, which offset the £4.35m projected rent revenue increase. If the hardship fund is not approved or is exhausted, the council may face increased arrears. A lender needs to know whether self-payer arrears are being actively monitored.
findings.figures: 69.94% of tenants eligible for HB/UC; 31.06% self-payers. Hardship fund: 119 residents with £59,500 historically; 61 residents with £30,500 in first half of 2025-26
findings.quote: It is estimated that 69.94% of tenants are eligible for some form of Housing Benefit (HB) or Universal Credit (UC). The remaining 31.06% receive no benefits and these self-payers could potentially be at some financial risk as a result of the increases.

findings.headline: The 2023-24 rent cap created a £57.1m net present value permanent loss with no recovery mechanism.
findings.detail: In 2023-24, the government capped social rent increases at 7% instead of the permitted 10.1% plus 1%. This £3.3m one-year loss compounds over the HRA's 30-year business plan to represent £57.1m of lost income at NPV 4%. The council explicitly states there is no mechanism to recoup this loss, permanently constraining the HRA's ability to invest in housing and meet statutory requirements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether an HRA's financial capacity has been permanently damaged by past government policy decisions. This £57.1m loss represents structural weakness in the housing business plan and may constrain future borrowing or investment capacity.
findings.figures: £3.3m loss in 2023-24; £57.1m net present value at 4% over 30-year business plan cycle
findings.quote: No mechanism was implemented to recoup the lost £3.3m revenue from 2023-24. At a Net Present Value (NPV) rate of 4%, over the 30-year business plan life cycle this equates to lost income of £57.1m to the HRA.

findings.headline: Croydon has deployed capital into a property fund investment.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has invested in the Real Lettings Property Fund Limited Partnership, a regulated property fund. This represents a longer-term capital commitment outside traditional liquid instruments. The document notes future property fund investments should only be considered after consulting treasury management advisers.
findings.matters: Property fund investments are illiquid, longer-term commitments with different return profiles and risk characteristics than government or bank deposits. A lender needs to know what capital is committed and for how long.
findings.figures: Real Lettings Property Fund Limited Partnership (named specifically as current investment)
findings.quote: The Council currently has invested in one property fund; the Real Lettings Property Fund Limited Partnership – see 3.5.13.

findings.headline: The council holds £206.5m in internal borrowing, risking liquidity constraints if cash is needed
findings.detail: From 2025/26 onwards, the council is holding a consistent £206.5m as internal borrowing—using cash reserves instead of external finance. While this temporarily reduces external debt, it erodes liquidity buffers and leaves the council vulnerable if revenue dips or capital needs spike unexpectedly.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing is not free: it consumes cash reserves that would otherwise cushion service disruptions or unexpected costs. A lender needs to know whether these reserves are committed elsewhere or whether they are genuinely available.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing: £160.8m (31/03/25 actual), £206.5m (31/03/26 forecast and beyond)
findings.quote: Internal borrowing 160.8 [31/03/25] 206.5 [31/03/26 onwards]

findings.headline: HRA debt burden is rising faster than revenues, with cost of servicing debt climbing to 18.1%
findings.detail: HRA debt is growing from £349.5m to £492.6m by 2028/29. The ratio of HRA debt to revenues rises from 3.6 to 4.4, and the ratio of cost of debt to revenue rises from 13.7% to 18.1%. This trajectory suggests the HRA business plan may come under pressure if revenues do not grow in line with debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: The HRA self-financing model depends on balancing debt with rentals and other revenues. A rising debt-to-revenue ratio at this pace (from 3.6 to 4.4 in five years) indicates the housing stock may become a drag on council finances if revenues stall.
findings.figures: HRA debt: £349.5m (2024/25) to £492.6m (2028/29); Debt to revenues ratio: 3.6 rising to 4.4; Cost of debt to revenue: 13.7% to 18.1%

findings.headline: Total debt is rising to £2.3bn over five years with capital commitments continuing at high levels
findings.detail: External debt is projected to grow from £1,279.5m to £1,868.7m. The Capital Financing Requirement rises from £1,834.9m to £2,328.1m by 2028/29. Capital expenditure remains high at £315.6m in 2025/26 and £321.3m in 2026/27, including £108.7m-£119.1m in Capitalisation Directions, which suggests ongoing use of one-off accounting treatments to manage budget pressures.
findings.matters: Rising debt coupled with sustained high capital spending and financing costs that are already unsustainable indicates the council may struggle to manage debt servicing without further revenue pressures or asset sales.
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement Projections... Total CFR 1,834.9 [2024/25] ... 2,328.1 [2028/29]

findings.headline: Financing costs are unsustainable and exceeding the council's own target by 80%
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges that debt financing costs are too high and not sustainable in the long term. The General Fund financing cost to net revenue stream ratio is currently 16.5% and forecast to remain between 17.7% and 18.5% through 2028/29, while the council's own sustainability target is under 10%. This gap persists across the entire forecast period with no recovery plan visible.
findings.matters: A council unable to service its debt within sustainable limits represents direct lending risk. A 7-8 percentage point shortfall against the council's own target signals either unsustainable capital plans or inadequate revenue resources.
findings.figures: General Fund financing cost/net revenue stream: 16.5% (2024/25 actual), 18.2% (2025/26 forecast), 17.7-18.5% (2026/27-2028/29); target: under 10%
findings.quote: It is acknowledged that the cost of servicing the Council's debt for the General Fund is too high and not sustainable in the long term and a ratio of Financing Costs to the Net Revenue Stream of under 10% should be targeted to ensure sustainability.

news_drafts.headline: Housing disrepair claims remain a material concern with costs growing despite management action.
news_drafts.lead: Disrepair claims represent both a financial and reputational risk. Awaab's Law creates a statutory obligation to fix hazards within tight timeframes, which could require emergency spending if the housing stock has widespread issues.

news_drafts.headline: Savings delivery achieved only 86.1% of target, with several initiatives deferred or cancelled.
news_drafts.lead: Savings delivery is a key test of whether a council can execute its financial recovery plan. Missing 13.9% of target, particularly where some savings are cancelled rather than delayed, suggests execution risk in achieving the planned deficits reduction.

news_drafts.headline: Croydon has not recovered value from historic asset investments including Fairfield Halls and Croydon Park Hotel.
news_drafts.lead: This shows a history of poor capital investment decisions where the council borrowed to acquire assets that have depreciated. The debt remains even as the asset value has fallen, indicating a structural problem in capital governance.
